title: ropeway:handbook-title-53
text: A shaft is the same cabin on the same rope, stood on end. Two stations in one column, one car, and a counterweight hanging on the other strand - so the drive lifts only the difference between them and not the car, which is why a lift runs on a mill that could not shift a ropeway up the same slope. Cliff or shaft - decide before you dig Build the steep leg as a ropeway if you have a cliff face: it keeps the view out, needs no new blocks and costs half the rope. What it will not do is match a shaft for speed, because it still pays the climb the counterweight cancels: on the four-sail mill this page recommends, a 70-degree span gains height at about half a shaft's rate, and even a maxed metal rotor only reaches about 86%. Sink a shaft when you have no room for the run - inside a tower, under a floor, or down a mine - where the lift is the only thing that fits. It is also the only steep machine in the mod that does not clip its own tower on the way past: a ropeway span over about 11 degrees drives the cabin's roof through its own crossarm, and a shaft station has no crossarm to drive it through. A shaft is eleven placed blocks, against thirty-two for a pair of ropeway stations. At the top: - 1 shaft head footing - 1 shaft sheave - 2 lay shafts - 1 drive head - 3 drive shafts - 1 drive housing At the bottom: - 1 shaft foot footing - 1 tension guide The machine, bottom to top Shaft foot footing on the floor of the shaft, facing the way you want the car's doors to open across. One tension guide three blocks along the way it faces - that is the counterweight's own lane, and its buffer. Shaft head footing at the top, in the same column, facing the same way - the link is refused if the two footings disagree, because the foot's facing is where you dug the guide and the head's is where the weight comes down. Above it: a shaft sheave four blocks up, facing the same way as the footing, then the drive leg three blocks to its right - a drive housing on the landing, three drive shafts, a drive head and two lay shafts back in to the sheave. That is the drive station's own machine leg, block for block, and an axle run into the housing drives it exactly as it drives a ropeway. Right-click either footing to see the whole of it standing there as see-through copies of the blocks themselves, before you place one of them. The hole Dig five columns along the head's facing by three across, centred on the two footings, from the block directly above the foot footing up to and including the sheave's own row, four blocks above the top landing. That whole box is the car's own body going past - not the rope's line - and the link is refused until it is clear. The four blocks above the top landing are part of it, so a top station roofed at three blocks is refused; so is a shaft sunk from the top that stops at the foot footing, which is where the car parks and where you sit. Then one more column, three along the facing from the axis, for the counterweight: nothing rides it, so it is not checked, and a player who skips it gets a counterweight that runs through stone and a lift that works. Leave the four cells above the sheave clear as well. The wheel is two and three quarter blocks across and it stands out over the shaft - that one is what the machine looks like rather than something the car needs, so nothing checks it. The top landing has a hole in it, and that is the machine The car parks with its floor level with the top landing and then goes down through it, so the landing has a car-sized opening and the head footing is an island in the middle of it. Step out at the top and you are put down on the nearest landing block - the lift knows where its own floor is. Step out at the bottom and you are on the pad, half a block down, exactly as at a ropeway tower. With the car at the bottom the counterweight stands above the top landing rather than below it - three and a half blocks of mass in the lane column, beside where you wait. That is simply where a counterweight is when the car is at the other end. It has no collision. Rope A shaft is charged double a ropeway's rope, because it really does hang two full-length strands: one to the car and one to the counterweight. A 40-block shaft is 20 haul rope. The rope is drawn between the car and the counterweight, so an empty shaft shows none of it - hang the cabin and the machine is finished. What it costs to run Nothing. A counterweighted car is the same load on your network as a level ropeway - the climb is cancelled by the weight rather than paid for - so a sheltered four-sail windmill runs a shaft at about 1.8 blocks of rise a second and a maxed metal one at about 3. A three-sail mill will do it in a good wind out of turbulence, and stall in a poor one. It does not beat a ladder door to door and it is not meant to: what it buys is no footprint, floors at one block each, and two riders with their freight. Rules the link enforces A shaft station links only to the other end of its own shaft - the same column, one head, the head on top, and both footings facing the same way. One span per footing, so one foot, one head and one car: there are no intermediate floors yet, and a shaft that folded back on itself would draw its counterweight below the bedrock. It will not link to a ropeway tower and a ropeway tower will not link to it. That is what keeps a lift a lift. Back to Aerial Ropeways, or Power and the Drive.
